title: PSYCH READING — What's tech doing to your brain?
author: C·E·L Mathayom

slides.title: What's tech doing to your brain?
slides.body: Let's read and find out.

slides.title: Grammar Entry Ticket
slides.body:
Answer the 15 questions on your paper.

You have 4 minutes.
slides.notes: 4-minute timer autostarts. Students complete the entry ticket silently. Then go through the answers one section at a time.

slides.title: Entry Ticket Answers — Part A
slides.body: 1. A2. C3. B4. D5. A
slides.notes: Q1 A — present perfect vs past simple. Q2 C — past continuous. Q3 B — first conditional. Q4 D — modal deduction (must). Q5 A — comparative with modifier (far bigger).

slides.title: Entry Ticket Answers — Part B
slides.body:
6. C7. B8. A9. D
10. A11. B12. B13. D
slides.notes: Q6 C — subject-verb agreement (sit→sits). Q7 B — plural marking (park→parks). Q8 A — comma splice. Q9 D — spelling (tomorow→tomorrow). Q10 A — there is/are (is→are). Q11 B — uncountable noun (advices→advice). Q12 B — apostrophe (its→it's). Q13 D — spelling (seperate→separate).

slides.title: Entry Ticket Answers — Part C
slides.body: 14. C15. C
slides.notes: Q14 C — modal perfect (leave→have left). Q15 C — third conditional (had avoided).

slides.title: Why is this lesson important?
slides.body:
• Your phone is part of your daily life. This topic affects you.
  • The evidence comes from real research on young people.
  • By the end, you will have your own opinion to write and share.
slides.notes: Frame the lesson value: technology touches every part of teens' lives, the evidence is real research, and the lesson ends with students forming and writing their own opinion.

slides.title: How do you use your phone?
slides.body:
How much time do you spend on it every day?

What do you do first when you wake up?

Do you ever scroll without thinking?

Opinion — Reason — Evidence
slides.notes: Open-class discussion, no right or wrong answers. Elicit freely. The yellow O-R-E label anchors the structure students will use for the final writing task.

slides.title: Choose Your Text
slides.body: Today you choose what you read.
slides.notes: Introduce the choice: three texts at three levels. Preview the excerpts, then students choose.

slides.body:
Which text will you read?

Preview each text, then choose your level.

B1

Roblox: A child-friendly game with a dark side

Main group with the teacher.
20 copies available.

B2

The hidden dangers of doomscrolling

Work together with a partner.
You mark your own answers.

C1

The truth about brain rot

Work together with a partner.
You mark your own answers.
slides.notes: Students choose their level. The main group stays on B1 (20 copies). B2 and C1 readers work in their own groups outside the main group and will self-mark with the printed answer guides.

slides.body:
B1

Roblox: A child-friendly game with a dark side

“When you open Roblox, it looks like a harmless game for children. The colourful blocks, the cute characters — everything seems friendly and safe. However, new research tells a very different story.”
slides.notes: A taste of the B1 text. Ask: does this sound interesting to you?

slides.body:
B2

The hidden dangers of doomscrolling

“When you wake up and reach for your phone, what do you do first? For many people, the answer is the same: they open a news app and start scrolling. Headline after headline brings bad news, yet the hand keeps moving.”
slides.notes: A taste of the B2 text. Ask: does this sound interesting to you?

slides.body:
C1

The truth about brain rot

“Most of us know the feeling of mindlessly scrolling through low-quality content. We call this sensation ‘brain rot.’ The term can also refer to the content itself: the absurdist, AI-generated characters and recycled memes that flood young people’s feeds.”
slides.notes: A taste of the C1 text. Ask: does this sound interesting to you?

slides.title: Let's Read
slides.body:
B1 readers: stay with the class.

B2 and C1 readers: work in your groups.
slides.notes: Direct students to their groups. B1 group works with the teacher. B2/C1 groups move together and work independently.

slides.body:
Listen & Read

Listen to the B1 text.
Follow along on your worksheet.

Then answer the 8 questions.
slides.notes: Play the B1 audio once (about 3 minutes). Students follow the text on the worksheet, then answer the 8 questions. B2 and C1 groups read their own texts silently and answer their own questions.

slides.title: Check Your Answers
slides.body:
B1: we check together.

B2 and C1: mark your own answers.
slides.notes: B1 answers are shown in the lesson. B2 and C1 students mark themselves with their answer guides.

slides.body:
B1 — Mark Your Answers

Check your own work. 60 seconds.

1. B2. C3. D4. C
5. A6. D7. B8. A

B2 and C1 readers: mark your own answers with your answer guide.
slides.notes: 60-second timer autostarts. Students mark their own sheets. B2/C1 groups self-mark with the printed answer guides. Then go through each question for explanations.

slides.title: B1 Answers (1/8)
slides.body:
Question1. According to the company, how many people played Roblox in 2024?
AnswerB. Over 85 million people used it daily.
ExplanationThe company reports that more than 85 million people played every day. The other options mix up the numbers, like the 40% who were under 13.
Transcript“In 2024, more than 85 million people played it every day, and about 40% of them were under 13.”

slides.title: B1 Answers (2/8)
slides.body:
Question2. What did the researchers discover about the accounts of young children?
AnswerC. Adults could message even the youngest accounts.
ExplanationThe researchers made fake accounts for pretend children. Even the five-year-old account could chat with adults. The platform could not tell how old anyone was.
Transcript“Children as young as five could chat with adults while playing.”

slides.title: B1 Answers (3/8)
slides.body:
Question3. What is the writer's purpose in writing this passage?
AnswerD. To show how easily children meet danger there.
ExplanationThe middle of the text describes the experiment and what the fake accounts could access. The writer uses these details to show that real dangers hide behind the friendly look.
Transcript“The ten-year-old's account could enter rooms that were clearly not suitable for children.”

slides.title: B1 Answers (4/8)
slides.body:
Question4. What is the main idea of paragraph 7?
AnswerC. The fixes still leave children exposed to strangers.
ExplanationThe paragraph says the new safety features do not go far enough. Children can still talk to strangers who are not on their friends list.
Transcript“Children can still talk to strangers who are not on their friends list.”

slides.title: B1 Answers (5/8)
slides.body:
Question5. In paragraph 4, what does the word “verification” mean?
AnswerA. Checking that information is true and correct.
ExplanationAge verification means proving that information, such as a player's age, is true. The text says no real verification existed, so nobody could check how old players were.
Transcript“It was impossible to know how old any player really was.”

slides.title: B1 Answers (6/8)
slides.body:
Question6. What does the passage suggest about Roblox's voice chat protection?
AnswerD. Players can get around it without much difficulty.
ExplanationThe report says the AI checks are easy to avoid. The researchers found that the filters did not catch the adult's request.
Transcript“The report says such measures are easy to avoid.”

slides.title: B1 Answers (7/8)
slides.body:
Question7. Many players are children, but the age checks fail. What does the writer suggest?
AnswerB. An adult can easily pretend to be a child.
ExplanationBecause there is no real way to check age, nobody can tell which players are adults and which are children. An adult can simply create an account and look like a young player.
Transcript“An adult account asked a five-year-old's account for personal details.”

slides.title: B1 Answers (8/8)
slides.body:
Question8. How does the writer feel about Roblox in the final paragraphs?
AnswerA. Critical of the company's efforts so far.
ExplanationThe writer ends by saying the company must do far more. That is a critical tone: the writer believes the efforts so far are not enough.
Transcript“It is time for the company to do far more, or for parents to think twice.”

slides.title: Time to Write
slides.body: All students write their own answer.
slides.notes: Everyone returns to their own work. All students write a 70-word response, whatever text they read.

slides.title: Structure Your Answer
slides.body:
OpinionI think technology changes the way I think.
ReasonOne reason is that I spend hours on my phone every day.
EvidenceFor example, the text shows how screens affect young people.

Opinion — Reason — Evidence
slides.notes: Model the structure with the example. Students use their own opinion, reason, and evidence from their own text (B1, B2, or C1).

slides.body:
Time to Write

Do you think technology is affecting your brain?

Write a 70-word response.

Opinion. Reason. Evidence from your text.
slides.notes: All students write a 70-word response. Use the O-R-E structure from the previous slide. Collect at the end of the lesson.
